name: Bright white
lede: Bright white is a pale, slightly greenish white whose Japanese library name, Aijiro, means "indigo white": the faintest trace of blue a dye vat can leave on cloth, and it reads only about 5 units from plain [[white]].

sections.title: Aijiro, the whitest shade of indigo
sections.body:
The Wikipedia survey "Traditional colors of Japan" lists this color under the romanized name Aijiro, written 藍白 [1]. 藍 names [[indigo]], the dye plant and its blue, and 白 is "white"; together the library glosses it as "indigo white," the near-colorless end of a dipped indigo gradation [1]. No book consulted here independently confirms a date, so the craft story beyond the gloss is undocumented [1].

Our library's own ISCC-NBS block for this swatch groups it with several other English near-white names, among them Birch and Surf Spray, which is a reminder of how many different names a single pale block of color can carry [1]. The nearest already-named color here is [[white]] itself, at a color-distance of 5.4 [1]. The hex, #EBF6F7, is a modern screen approximation, not a measurement of dyed cloth [1].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
A color within range of this swatch appears in 79 of the 23,781 paintings in our archive, about 0.33 percent, as photographed; the within-painting lens finds it in 54 [2]. That is more common than 51 percent of the named colors we track, so this pale white sits roughly in the middle of our rarity scale [2].

It peaks in the 1900s, present in 9 of 1,674 paintings from that century, 1.9 times the expected rate [2]. Inside a painting it most often plays a light, in nearly three-quarters of the paintings that carry it [2]. The earliest dated appearance we have is Ambrogio Lorenzetti, 1332, though the archive's early centuries are thin, so this is a floor and not a true first sighting [2].
